course.title: Knowledge Graphs
course.subtitle: Retrieval is not reasoning over connections. Thirteen parts, four phases, graded.
course.note: Built from the daVault curriculum: kg-agentic-graph-design-course-checklist.md and the compressed crash course. Every wrong answer returns the correction and the reason.
howto: Four phases, thirteen parts, 44 graded items. Phase 1 is manual extraction with no model, because you cannot evaluate an extractor you have never beaten by hand.
Each part has a lesson, a sample text when the part needs one, instructions, then items. Jump anywhere from the left rail.
Every wrong answer shows what you wrote, what the right shape is, and why. Your best score per item is kept, and every miss lands in the error log.
Part mastery is the average of your best scores. Anything under 100 percent sits in Review, where you can drill it.
The phase gates from the vault are encoded as items: retrieval versus reasoning, one false merge plus one missed merge, and a decision path you can reconstruct state by state.

phases.label: Proof
phases.note: Weeks 7-10. The failure log is the deliverable.

modules.title: Retrieval is not reasoning
modules.goal: Say in one sentence what a graph does that document search cannot.

text.title: Three support tickets
text.body:
Ticket #1041 (Mar 2): Billing doubled after I upgraded to Pro. Alex from support said the old Basic plan wasn't canceled.

Ticket #1042 (Mar 3): Alex reactivated my Basic plan and refunded March. Upgrade to Pro now works.

Ticket #1047 (Mar 5): Can't export to CSV. Support told me it's a known bug with the Pro plan's export tool.

lesson.x: Retrieval finds text similar to your question. A knowledge graph represents the actual chain of connected things: ticket, then defective part, then product line, then supplier, then shipment batch, then root cause. The first hands you chunks and leaves you to connect them. The second traverses connections for you.
Why the distinction decides everything downstream

If you believe retrieval is reasoning, you will build a chunk index, call it RAG, and then wonder why the answer to a cross-document question is a confident paragraph with no chain behind it. Every later decision, the schema, the resolve step, the provenance, the citation rule, exists to make the chain real.
The vault gate for this phase: can you explain retrieval versus following a chain of connected facts, using your own text as the example? If not, redo the exercise with a different text set.

x: Retrieval answers: here are passages that look like your question
A graph answers: here is the path from A to B, and here is each edge on it
The tell: a question with no wording overlap with its answer needs connections, not similarity

instructions: Read the three tickets first. They are the sample text for the whole of Phase 1.
Three items: one about what search returns, one about which questions need a graph, one about the one-sentence test.
Multiple choice answers click once and lock. A retry button appears after grading.

exercises.prompt: You ask: which supplier caused the returns spike. What does vector retrieval give you?
options: Passages that mention suppliers and returns. You still connect them yourself.
The chain from the affected part to the supplier and the shipment batch.
A ranked list of suppliers with a causal score.
Nothing, because the question spans several documents.
exercises.why: Similarity returns similar text. The connection between a return rate and a supplier lives in the structure, not in any single passage, so retrieval can only hand you the pieces.
wrong: That is the graph's answer, and only if the edges were extracted and resolved first.
Retrieval ranks similarity, it does not compute causality. A ranked list is a different system.
It returns something: the passages that talk about suppliers and returns. The gap is the connectivity, not the coverage.

exercises.prompt: Which of these questions actually need a graph rather than a document index?
options: Which suppliers of Zarya Energy share a board member with Kestrel Robotics?
Summarise the risks in this one contract.
What does the docs page say about retry behaviour?
Which tickets were handled by the same agent who later worked on the CSV export bug?
notes: Two hops through two organisations and a shared person across documents. No chunk contains it.
Single document, summarisation. Retrieval handles this well and the graph adds cost.
A lookup inside one page. Embeddings, or even grep, are enough.
The connection is a shared actor across tickets. Reads like a search, resolves only as a join.
exercises.why: The test is whether the answer exists in one place. If it is assembled from separate records by following relations, a graph earns its cost.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence states the distinction correctly?
options: Retrieval returns text that resembles the question; a graph returns the path between things, with each edge named and sourced.
A graph is a faster index over the same chunks.
A graph stores embeddings next to documents so search is more accurate.
A graph lets the model read more documents per query.
exercises.why: The difference is structural, not speed or accuracy. Paths and named edges are what a chunk index does not have.
wrong: Same chunks, same index, no path. Speed is not the distinction.
Embeddings next to documents is still retrieval. The adjacency is what changes the answer.
Context size is a budget question, not a knowledge-graph question.

modules.title: Entities are things, not verbs
modules.goal: Separate the things in a passage from the relationships around them.

lesson.x: An entity is a thing you can point at twice: a person, a product, a feature, an organisation, an event, a place. Billing, support and upgraded are not entities. They are relationships and context wearing noun clothing, and adding them is the most common way a schema leaks.
The list you should produce by hand

Alex          person
Basic plan    product
Pro plan      product
CSV export    feature
Ticket #1041  event
March         time

For each entity, note three things: the canonical name you will use, its type, and the variants the text uses for it. The variant list is what the Resolve stage will need later, so collect it while you are reading rather than guessing afterwards.
Judgment test: would it make sense to say 'tell me everything connected to X'? For Alex, yes. For upgraded, the question is meaningless. That question separates entities from everything else.

instructions: Use the three tickets from Part 1. Open it from the rail if you need to reread them.
The multiple-select item gives partial credit and every wrong selection cancels a correct one, so do not select something you are unsure of.
The sorting item scores per card. The last item is a schema-leak diagnosis.

exercises.prompt: Which of these are entities in the three tickets?
options: Alex
Basic plan
March
upgraded
billing
CSV export
notes: A person, named and persistent across tickets. Entity.
A product. Another ticket refers to it as 'the plan I had before', so it needs a canonical name and variants.
A time period referenced by two tickets. A thing of type time, or a literal on an event, but a thing.
A verb in the past tense. It is the relationship between a customer and a plan, not a node.
A topic. It appears as the object of 'reports', never as something you can connect to.
A feature with a known bug. Entity, and the object of the export relation.
exercises.why: Four things and two non-things. The judgment is the skill: nouns like billing and support read like entities and are not.

exercises.prompt: Type each entity you kept from the tickets.

items.note: A support agent. Type person, with a role that is itself a relation.
Type product. It appears as Basic, 'the old Basic plan' and 'the plan I had before'.
Type feature. It is the object of the bug relation, not a product on its own.
Type event. Tickets are events with a date, a reporter and a set of relations.

exercises.why: Types are what let the validator reject bad triples later. A product cannot be the agent of a support action, and knowing that costs nothing at extraction time.

exercises.prompt: Your extractor emits 'support' as an entity of type Organisation. What is wrong?
options: It is a function or department in this text, not an organisation. The schema is leaking relationship words into the entity list.
Nothing. Support is a department, so Organisation is correct.
It should be type Person, because a person answered.
It should be merged with Alex.
exercises.why: Nothing in the tickets names a support organisation. 'Support told me' is a speech relation with an unnamed speaker. Emitting it as an entity creates a node that no fact can attach to correctly.
wrong: A departmental label in a customer sentence is not an organisation node. The tell is that no ticket gives it a name.
The person is Alex, named in two other tickets. Support is the channel, not the person.
Merging a channel with a person is a false merge, and it destroys the evidence that the speaker was unnamed.

modules.title: Triples from the tickets
modules.goal: Write one fact per line, with a predicate that is a relation.

lesson.x: A triple is subject, predicate, object: one fact, one line. The subject and object are entities, the predicate is a relation type from your schema. The predicate is where most hand-written extraction fails, because the natural-language verb is rarely the relation you want.
The worked example

alex         | handles      | ticket_1041
alex         | reactivated  | basic_plan
ticket_1047  | involves     | csv_export
csv_export   | bugged_in    | pro_plan

Note what each line refuses to do. 'Billing doubled' is not a triple, it is a symptom with no second entity. 'Upgraded to Pro' produces two possible relations and the ticket only supports the cancellation one. A triple you cannot point at a sentence for is a triple you invented.
If a line needs the word 'and' to be true, it is two triples. If it needs a date, a role or a source, it is an event node, which is Part 7.

instructions: Use the three tickets from Part 1 as the only source. Do not add anything from the world.
Format: subject | predicate | object, one fact per line. Example: alex | handles | ticket_1041
Write exactly four lines for the first item. Case, underscores, hyphens, hashes and diacritics are ignored, so ticket_1041, ticket 1041 and #1041 all match.
Predicates are matched against a short synonym list: handles, handled and responded to all count for the same relation.
Each expected triple is worth a quarter. Every extra line you cannot match costs an eighth, so padding with guesses lowers your score.

exercises.prompt: Write the four core facts from the three tickets.
exercises.why: Four assertions, four lines. Billing, March, upgraded and support belong to none of them: they are symptoms, times and verbs. If you wrote a line for 'billing doubled', ask what its object is. There is none, and that is the signal.
exercises.hint: Lower case, one fact per line, three fields separated by a pipe.

exercises.prompt: Which word from the tickets is a relation type rather than a topic?
options: handles
billing
support
upgraded
exercises.why: Handles takes two entities and asserts something between them. Billing is a topic, support is a channel, and upgraded is a verb describing a change that only becomes a fact once you name both the plan and the date.
wrong: A topic. You can report on billing, but nothing connects to it.
A channel or a function. No entity in the tickets is named by it.
A verb, but not a relation type yet: upgrading is a change of plan, and you need the from and to plans before it is a triple.

exercises.prompt: Which of these are legitimate triples for the three tickets?
options: alex | handles | ticket_1042
pro plan | caused | billing issue
csv export | bugged in | pro plan
ticket_1047 | involves | csv export
basic plan | upgraded to | pro plan
notes: Ticket #1042 opens with Alex reacting, and #1041 says Alex was the support contact. Supported.
The tickets say billing doubled and that a plan was not cancelled. They never assert causation. This is the invented-causal-edge failure, and it is the one that reads most convincingly.
Stated: a known bug with the Pro plan's export tool.
Stated directly.
Direction and predicate are both unsupported. The customer upgraded; the plans did not upgrade each other.
exercises.why: Three supported, two invented. The causal one is the important catch: an extractor that adds causes is not being helpful, it is fabricating the part of the graph people will trust most.

modules.title: The chain search cannot show
modules.kicker: Draw it, then say what it proves
modules.goal: Trace a path across documents and name what it reveals that per-document search does not.

lesson.x: Draw circles for entities and arrows for predicates. The picture is not the deliverable. What the picture shows is: one person, Alex, sits on both the billing failure and the CSV bug, across two tickets that share no wording. A document search returns those tickets separately, or returns neither.
The long chain, from the vault
support ticket -> defective part -> product line -> supplier -> shipment batch -> root cause

Six nodes. No single document contains the whole path, and no embedding of the question is close to any of the six. That is the shape of every question a graph is for: the answer is a path, and the path is the evidence.
Phase 1 gate: you cannot pass this phase on definitions alone. Point at one entity in your own text and walk the chain that retrieval would miss.

instructions: Three items: what the drawing reveals, the order of the long chain, and one implied connection.
The ordering item is all or nothing. Click steps into the sequence and click a step in the sequence to remove it.
For the implied-connection item, pick the connection the text supports by inference and nothing stronger.

exercises.prompt: What does the drawn graph show that searching the three tickets separately cannot?
options: That the same support agent, Alex, is on both the billing failure and the CSV bug.
That billing doubled after the upgrade.
That the Pro plan has an export bug.
That the customer is unhappy.
exercises.why: The shared node is the whole point. Two tickets that never reference each other, joined by one person, which is exactly the structure a chunk index flattens away.
wrong: That fact sits inside one ticket. Search finds it.
Also inside one ticket.
An inference from tone, not a fact in the graph. Sentiment is a different extraction problem.

exercises.prompt: Order the causal chain from the symptom to the root cause.
exercises.why: Symptom first, cause last, each hop a named relation. Reversing it is how you end up with a graph that can only answer questions you already knew the answer to.

exercises.prompt: Which connection is supported by inference from the tickets, without inventing a fact?
options: Alex already has context on both the billing issue and the CSV export bug.
Alex caused the CSV export bug.
The CSV bug and the billing issue share a root cause.
The Pro plan is defective.
exercises.why: It is a statement about the graph structure, not about the world: one node appears on two paths. Every other option asserts causation or a shared cause that no ticket states.
wrong: Nothing connects Alex to the bug except handling a ticket about it. This is the causal leap to refuse.
Plausible, unsupported. Two problems handled by one person is not one root cause.
A product with a known bug is not a defective product. That escalation is how a graph starts lying in a confident voice.

modules.title: Extract: schema before prose
modules.kicker: One cheap call per document, strict JSON
modules.goal: Define the extraction contract so the model cannot return topics as entities.

lesson.x: Extract is one cheap model call per document returning structured JSON. The schema is the control surface: entities carry type and canonical_name, triples carry subject, predicate and object that reference those canonical names. No freeform text, no invented relationships.
The contract

Two rules do most of the work. One fact per triple, so a line containing 'and' is rejected. And a closed predicate list, because an open one produces employed_by, works_for and employee_at for the same relation and fractures your graph into three.

The ten-minute gate from the vault: diff the model output against a document you extracted by hand. Any entity that is really a relationship means the schema is leaking. Fix the schema, rerun. Do not fix the output.

instructions: Four items: a schema leak, invalid output, the slot each field belongs to, and the pipeline order.
For the invalid-output item, select every record that breaks the contract. Partial credit, and a wrong selection cancels a right one.
The leaking-schema item is the important one: the answer is always to fix the schema, not to patch the output.

exercises.prompt: The extractor returns an entity of type Organisation named 'support'. What is the right fix?
options: Tighten the schema: restrict entity types and add a rule that a role or channel is not an entity.
Delete that entity in a post-processing pass.
Add 'support' to a blocklist of forbidden entity names.
Accept it: extra entities do not affect the triples.
exercises.why: A blocklist treats one symptom. The schema change removes the class of error, and it is the only fix that survives the next document with a different channel word.
wrong: Post-processing hides the leak and must be maintained forever, per document.
You will be adding blocked words for the rest of the project. The type restriction is one line.
Extra entity nodes become the objects of wrong triples, and every later join inherits them.

exercises.prompt: Which extractor records break the contract?
options: entity: {type: 'topic', name: 'billing'}
entity: {type: 'product', canonical_name: 'basic_plan'}
triple: {subject: 'alex', predicate: 'handles', object: 'ticket_1041 and ticket_1047'}
triple: {subject: 'alex', predicate: 'said', object: 'the old Basic plan was not canceled'}
notes: Two breaks: a topic type that should not exist in the schema, and no canonical_name field.
Valid. Type plus canonical name is exactly the contract.
Two objects in one object field. One fact per triple, so this is two triples written as one.
The object is a freeform sentence, not a canonical entity. Either extract the claim's entities or drop it.
exercises.why: Three breaks, one valid. Note that the sentence-shaped object is the subtle one: it looks like careful extraction and it is unusable for any join.

exercises.prompt: Which slot does each piece of an extraction record belong to?

items.note: The stable key the whole graph joins on.
Person, product, feature, event. The type is what the validator checks domain and range against.
A relation type from the closed list, never the surface verb.
Provenance, recorded per triple at assembly. It is not part of the extractor's entity or triple contract.

exercises.why: Keeping the extraction contract small is what makes it enforceable. Provenance is attached later, at assembly, and mixing it into the extractor prompt makes the model editorialise.

exercises.prompt: Order the four stages from one document to a cited answer.
items: Extract entities and triples as structured JSON
Query the subgraph and cite edges
exercises.why: Extract, resolve, assemble, query. Resolve before assemble, because assembling first welds alias variants into separate nodes and every downstream join inherits the split.

modules.title: Resolve: same thing, different words
modules.kicker: The stage where the errors hide
modules.goal: Catch a false merge and a missed merge, and explain why they are not equally bad.

lesson.x: Resolve clusters entity variants using context and description, not string matching. The killer case from the vault is Edwin Aldrin and Buzz Aldrin: the same person, zero shared tokens. String similarity scores that pair at zero and a lookup table never sees it.
Two error classes, both must be found

x: False merge: two different things welded into one node. Every fact attached afterwards is contaminated and the fix means replaying history.
Missed merge: the same thing left as two nodes. Visible, joinable later, annoying rather than destructive.

lesson.x: Because the costs are asymmetric, the operational answer is a review band: auto-merge the confident pairs, auto-reject the clear negatives, and send the middle to a human with the evidence attached. That band is also where your labelled data comes from.
The vault gate for Weeks 3-4: show one extraction error you caught, one resolve error you caught, and what you changed. If you cannot show both, you rushed the phase.

instructions: Four items: which pairs you would merge, the zero-overlap case, the asymmetry term, and the threshold policy.
For pairs, select only what you would merge automatically. A pair you would send to review is not a selection.
Partial credit on pairs, with each wrong selection cancelling a right one.

exercises.prompt: Which pairs are the same entity, resolvable without human review?
options: Edwin Aldrin / Buzz Aldrin
Basic plan / the plan I had before
Pro / the paid tier
Kestrel Robotics / Kestrel Systems
notes: Same person: same missions, same dates, same crew. Zero string overlap, and the context is unambiguous.
The second ticket refers back to the plan named in the first. Co-reference across documents, resolvable from the thread.
The ticket says the customer upgraded to Pro, then calls it the paid tier. Same node, different register.
Different second token, different legal entity. This is the false merge a name-prefix matcher makes, and it is unrecoverable in practice.
exercises.why: Three true merges, one trap. The trap looks more similar than the first option and is the one that must not merge. Similarity is not identity.

exercises.prompt: Edwin Aldrin and Buzz Aldrin share zero tokens. What actually resolves them?
options: Context and description: same missions, same dates, same crew, same role.
A nickname dictionary.
Phonetic matching.
Embedding similarity on the two names alone.
exercises.why: The evidence is around the names, not in them. That is why resolve needs the document text, and why a resolve stage fed only entity strings is working blind.
wrong: A dictionary works for the pairs you thought of and fails on the next thousand.
Phonetics gets you Edwin and Edward, which is the wrong direction.
Embeddings of two short names carry almost no signal, and the pair shares no subword structure to exploit.

exercises.prompt: Fill the blank with the error you should prefer when the matcher is unsure.
exercises.sentence: A merged pair is expensive to undo once triples attach to it, so when the matcher is unsure the cheap error is a ______ rather than a false merge.

blanks.note: A missed merge leaves two nodes you can link later. A false merge poisons one node and every edge on it, and the fix is a replay.

exercises.why: Asymmetric cost. Tune toward precision on merges, accept visible duplicates, and let the review band resolve the middle. Splitting is a cleanup; welding is a migration.

exercises.prompt: Your matcher auto-merges 1,200 pairs and 180 are wrong. Most defensible change?
options: Raise the auto-merge threshold and route the 0.75 to 0.95 band to human review with the evidence attached.
Lower the threshold so recall improves, then clean up later.
Merge only on shared identifiers.
Keep merging and log the errors.
exercises.why: Fifteen percent contamination is a correctness problem, and a review band converts the ambiguous middle into decisions while producing the labelled pairs you need to tune at all.
wrong: Lowering the threshold trades a cleanup for a replay, in the expensive direction.
Shared identifiers are rare. You would lose most true matches and the graph fragments.
Logging does not stop contamination. Every triple attached to a bad node must be replayed after the fix.

modules.title: Assemble: typed edges and provenance
modules.kicker: Canonical nodes, one source per fact
modules.goal: Land the graph so every edge can be traced to the sentence that produced it.

lesson.x: Assemble takes canonical nodes, typed edges and a provenance record on every triple: source document, character span, extractor version, confidence, timestamp. Provenance is not metadata you add later. It is the thing that lets you review an extraction, detect a regression after a prompt change, and decide which source wins when two disagree.
Qualified facts become nodes

action_1 | type    | SupportAction
action_1 | agent   | alex
action_1 | affects | basic_plan
action_1 | date    | 2024-03-03

In RDF an edge cannot hold agent, date and object at once, so the relation becomes a node. In a property graph you may put these on the edge instead, which is faster to write and impossible to port. Choose per project, but choose deliberately.
Quarantine beats deletion. A low-confidence triple with no source is a question, not an error. Park it in a holding graph until a person or a better source settles it.

instructions: Four items: the RDF versus property-graph choice, building an event node, what must carry provenance, and the missing provenance field.
For the event item write exactly four lines with the node id action_1. Field names lower case.
Partial credit on the event item: a quarter per correct field, minus an eighth per extra line.

exercises.prompt: You must publish to plain RDF, no RDF-star. How do you store 'Alex reactivated the Basic plan on 3 March'?
options: An event node carrying agent, affects and date, with the plan hanging off that node.
One triple alex reactivated basic_plan, plus a comment with the date.
A triple per qualifier, all hanging off Alex.
Put the date in the predicate name, reactivated_on_2024_03_03.
exercises.why: Without edge annotations, promoting the relation to a node is the only lossless shape. It also gives you something to attach the ticket and the document span to later.
wrong: Comments are not data. The date is lost to every query.
Qualifiers on the person become claims about the person forever, so the history goes wrong when the next action arrives.
Predicate names become an unbounded vocabulary, and the schema stops being enforceable.

exercises.prompt: Write the four core triples of the action node. Use the id action_1.
exercises.why: Four fields: what it is, who did it, what it touched, when. The date is a literal on the event, which is the point of the event existing. Ask what Alex did in March and this answers it without reading the ticket.
exercises.hint: The event node is the subject of all four lines.

exercises.prompt: Which triples must carry provenance before you trust them?
options: A triple produced by a model extraction pass.
A triple a person typed in by hand from ticket #1041.
A triple created by merging facts from two documents.
A triple derived by a query over existing edges.
notes: Model output without a span cannot be reviewed, so you can never measure or correct it.
Hand entry is right more often, not always. Without the span nobody can re-check it and nobody knows it changed.
A merge is a claim about identity. It needs the evidence that justified it or it cannot be undone.
A derived fact inherits its inputs. If it cannot point at them, a wrong answer has nowhere to be traced.
exercises.why: All four. Provenance is uniform or it is decoration: the moment one class skips it, a query that joins across classes has an unverifiable branch.

exercises.prompt: Fill the missing provenance field.
exercises.sentence: Each triple records the source document, the extractor version, a confidence, and the character ______ it was taken from.

blanks.note: The span is what makes a triple reviewable: click it and the source sentence highlights. Without it, 'is this extraction correct' has no answer.

exercises.why: A fact you cannot highlight is a fact you cannot correct at scale, and correction at scale is the whole job.

modules.title: Query: serialize and cite
modules.goal: Make the answer trace to specific edges, and refuse when it cannot.

lesson.x: Query takes the relevant subgraph, serialises it as triples, and lets the model reason over those triples. The output rule is what separates a graph system from RAG with extra steps: the answer cites edges by name, or it does not answer.
Two answers to the same question

bad:  Based on the support tickets, Alex may have caused the billing issue.
good: edge[alex -> handles -> ticket_1041] and edge[ticket_1041 -> reports -> billing_issue]
      show one agent on both paths. Causation is not asserted by any edge.

The bad answer is fluent, unsupported and shaped like insight. It is also the default output of a system that was given chunks instead of edges. The good answer is dull and checkable, which is the trade you are making.
Rule: if the model cannot cite an edge, it does not answer. An honest miss is worth more than a confident paragraph nobody can verify.

instructions: Four items: which answer is grounded, when a graph earns its cost, the retrieval order, and one unsupported claim.
The ordering item is all or nothing.
Read every option against the rule: cite an edge or do not answer.

exercises.prompt: Which answer is grounded in the graph?
options: edge[ticket_1042 -> handled_by -> alex] and edge[ticket_1041 -> handled_by -> alex] mean Alex is on both tickets.
Based on the tickets, the billing issue and the export bug are probably related.
The customer upgraded and had several problems, including billing and CSV export.
Alex caused the billing issue by not cancelling the Basic plan.
exercises.why: Named edges, and a claim that does not exceed them. The other three are fluent and none can be checked against a specific pair of nodes.
wrong: Probably is the tell. No edge says related, so the claim has no source.
A summary of topics, not a path. It reads well and answers nothing specific.
The tickets say the plan was not cancelled, not that Alex failed to cancel it. This is the causal leap that survives review because it sounds like diagnosis.

exercises.prompt: Which question justifies a graph over a chunk index?
options: Which customers hit the CSV export bug and also had a billing change handled by the same agent?
Summarise this ticket.
What does the help page say about exports?
Find tickets similar to this one.
exercises.why: Two conditions joined through a shared actor across records. The others are single-document or similarity tasks where retrieval is cheaper and just as good.
wrong: One document. Summarisation is retrieval's home ground.
A lookup in one page.
That is literally what embeddings do, and they do it well.

exercises.prompt: Order the query steps.
items: Link the question's entities to canonical nodes
Rank candidate triples by confidence and provenance
Require the answer to cite the edges it used
exercises.why: Link, expand, rank, serialise, cite. Drop the ranking and low-confidence edges flood the context. Drop the citation and a wrong answer is indistinguishable from a right one.

exercises.prompt: The model answers 'the tickets suggest Alex may have caused the billing problem'. What is the defect?
options: No edge asserts causation, so the claim is unsupported and must be refused or restated as the edges that do exist.
The model should have read more tickets.
Causation is fine to infer if confidence is above 0.8.
The answer needs a longer explanation.
exercises.why: The graph holds handles and reports. Causation is not in it. The correct behaviour is to answer with the path that exists and say plainly that the causal link is not in the data.
wrong: More documents do not create an edge. Coverage does not fix an unsupported inference.
Confidence scores the extraction of existing edges, not the invention of new relation types.
Length is not grounding. A longer unsupported answer is worse, because it reads more authoritative.

modules.title: Three commitments
modules.goal: Apply explicit structure to the agent, not just the data.

lesson.x: The second half of the course is the same idea pointed at the agent. Replace opaque hidden decisions with explicit structure: states with triggers, instead of a loop where the model decides what happens next.
The three commitments

x: Immutable plan: the plan locks once generated. No mid-run improvisation. Trades flexibility for auditability.
Separated layers: planning, execution and recovery are independent roles, and the agent does not grade its own work.
Strict escalation: recovery follows a fixed protocol with a hard retry limit, not infinite retries.

lesson.x: Each commitment costs something real. You give up the ability to replan when step 4 goes wrong, in exchange for a decision path you can reconstruct afterwards. For a system whose output people rely on, that trade is usually correct, and it is always a decision rather than a default.
Same shape in both halves: a digraph of decisions in the data, a digraph of states in the agent. If you can only explain one, you built half a course.

instructions: Three items: spot a violated commitment, select the commitments themselves, and name the trade-off.
Partial credit on the multi-select, with cancellation for wrong selections.
Distractors in the multi-select are practices that sound rigorous and are not one of the three.

exercises.prompt: Which run violates the immutable plan commitment?
options: The agent rewrites its plan at step 3 because step 2 returned unexpected data, then continues.
The agent stops after two failed retries and escalates to a human with the errors attached.
The verifier is a different model from the executor.
Every state transition is appended to a log with its trigger.
exercises.why: Replanning mid-run is exactly what the commitment forbids. The plan locks, and a surprise becomes a recovery or an escalation, not a new plan.
wrong: That is strict escalation working as designed.
Separated layers: the builder does not grade its own work.
That is the property that makes the whole thing auditable.

exercises.prompt: Which of these are the three commitments?
options: Immutable plan: the plan locks once generated.
Separated layers: planning, execution and recovery are independent roles.
Strict escalation: fixed recovery protocol with a hard retry limit.
Maximum parallelism: all available tools fire in one step.
Self-grading: the executor scores its own output before finishing.
notes: Auditability comes from the plan not moving under you.
The agent that does the work is not the one that judges it.
Bounded retries force a decision instead of a loop.
Parallelism is a performance choice. It is not a commitment about structure.
The opposite of separated layers, and the most common way the guarantee is quietly lost.
exercises.why: Three commitments, two plausible-sounding non-commitments. A list of good practices is not a design guarantee, and the difference is whether a rule can be violated.

exercises.prompt: What does the immutable plan cost you?
options: Flexibility: a surprise mid-run cannot produce a new plan, only a recovery or an escalation.
Speed, because the plan must be regenerated each step.
Accuracy, because the plan is never checked.
Nothing. It is strictly better than a replanning agent.
exercises.why: You trade improvisation for a decision path you can reconstruct. Saying the trade out loud is the difference between a design decision and a cargo cult.
wrong: The plan is generated once. Costing less is the point.
It is checked more, not less, because it cannot change to hide an error.
Nothing is strictly better. A genuinely novel situation is where the replanning agent wins.

modules.title: States, triggers, escalation
modules.kicker: The graph you draw around the agent
modules.goal: Write the five states and the trigger on every transition.

lesson.x: You design the agent as a graph: Planning, Executing step N, Recovering, Escalated, Complete. Every transition has a specific trigger. No state change happens because the model felt like it.

Planning    -> Executing 1   when the plan is written and frozen
Executing N -> Executing N+1 when step N verifies
Executing N -> Recovering    when step N fails
Recovering  -> Executing N   when retries < 2
Recovering  -> Escalated     when the retry limit is hit
Executing N -> Complete      when all steps verify

Then run the same task twice: once with these states and rules given to the agent, once as one loose prompt. The difference you are measuring is not quality. It is whether you can explain why the system did what it did at each step.
Choose the retry limit deliberately and write down the reasoning. Two is a decision about cost and context, not a magic number, and you should be able to defend it.

instructions: Four items: order the states, name the escalation trigger, set the retry limit, defend it.
The numeric item accepts a plain number.
The ordering item is all or nothing.

exercises.prompt: Order the states of one run that ends with a handoff.
exercises.why: Every state is a position you can name after the fact. If the sequence cannot be written down, the transitions are not explicit and the run is opaque no matter how good the output looked.

exercises.prompt: What triggers the move from Recovering to Escalated?
options: The fixed retry limit is reached and the last attempt still fails.
The model reports low confidence in its own output.
The task takes longer than usual.
A tool returns an unexpected value.
exercises.why: Escalation is a budget event, not a feeling. It fires when the protocol is exhausted, which is why the limit has to be a number written down in advance.
wrong: The agent does not grade its own work, and confidence is not a state trigger.
Duration is a resource signal, and if it matters it needs its own explicit transition rule.
An unexpected value is what puts you into Recovering in the first place.

exercises.prompt: How many retries does the strict escalation protocol allow before handing off? Give the number.
exercises.why: Two. The limit exists to convert a loop into a decision, and the reasoning matters more than the value: a third attempt costs more than the information it adds, and a handoff with two failure records is more useful to a human than a longer transcript.
exercises.hint: The same limit the vault uses for the worker pipeline.

exercises.prompt: Why a hard retry limit instead of letting the agent retry until it succeeds?
options: Because an unbounded loop spends budget without producing a decision, and the escalation is more useful with two failure records than with twenty.
Because models degrade after two attempts.
Because retries are cheap but slow.
Because a limit makes the run faster.
exercises.why: The limit is about converting a loop into an accountable decision. Two failures with inputs and errors is a solvable problem; a long transcript of the same failure is not.
wrong: There is no universal degradation at two. The number is a design choice about cost and signal.
Retries are not cheap, and cost is not the main argument.
A hard limit often makes the run slower per attempt, because it forces the handoff. Speed is not the goal.

modules.title: Reconstruct the path
modules.goal: Read a run log and say exactly where the design failed.

text.title: Run log
text.body:
plan written: 4 steps
step 1 ok
step 2 failed: schema mismatch
replanning: 3 new steps
step 1 (new plan) ok
step 2 (new plan) failed: same schema mismatch
replanning again
step 1 (third plan) failed
result: gave up, no handoff, no escalation record

lesson.x: The gate after Week 6 is not did it work. It is: can you reconstruct the full decision path from memory, state by state? A log you cannot turn into a state sequence means the transitions were never explicit.
What the log above proves

Three plans, the same failure twice, and no escalation record. The agent replanned instead of recovering, which breaks the immutable plan. It then had no bounded recovery, which breaks strict escalation. And there is no verdict from a separate layer, so nobody established whether the work was good.
A useful failure log records, per attempt: the state, the trigger that moved it, the input, what changed, and whether the fix held. Anything less and the log cannot settle an argument.

instructions: Three items about the run log: which commitment broke, what the correct state sequence was, and what the log is missing.
For the missing-information item, select only fields a reviewer would need to settle the case.
Partial credit with cancellation.

exercises.prompt: Which commitment did this run break first?
options: Immutable plan: it replanned twice instead of recovering within the frozen plan.
Separated layers: the same agent planned and executed.
Strict escalation: it gave up without a handoff.
None. It failed for a technical reason.
exercises.why: The first violation is the replan at step 2. Everything after it follows: a moving plan cannot have a bounded recovery, because the recovery is against a target that keeps changing.
wrong: A real concern, but the log does not show it, and the replan happens first.
The missing escalation is the second violation, downstream of the first.
It did fail technically. The design failure is how the system responded to that failure.

exercises.prompt: What should the sequence have been after step 2 failed?
exercises.why: Failure goes to recovery, recovery is bounded, and the bound produces an escalation with evidence. Replanning is not on this path at all.

exercises.prompt: What is missing from this log for a reviewer to settle the case?
options: The state name for every line.
The trigger that caused each transition.
The actual input and error text per attempt.
Whether the fix held after the retry.
The model temperature.
notes: Lines without states cannot be assembled into a path.
Without the trigger, a transition looks like a mood rather than a rule.
Two identical failures cannot be told apart from two different ones without the text.
This is the only line that answers whether the recovery worked.
A setting, not evidence about this run. It belongs in the run config, not the failure record.
exercises.why: Four required fields, one red herring. The failure record is the artifact a reviewer argues with, so it needs state, trigger, evidence and outcome.

modules.title: The failure log is the deliverable
modules.goal: Know what makes a project count as evidence of understanding.

lesson.x: The portfolio phase asks for 50 to 100 real documents, a working pipeline, an agent that queries the graph, and an honest failure log. The log is the part that cannot be faked and the part reviewers actually read.
The five ways this stalls

x: Skipping the manual extraction phase, so you can run extraction but cannot evaluate it
Treating resolve as solved, when most errors hide there
Building only one half, the graph or the agent
Polishing the demo instead of documenting failure
Waiting for a graph architect job posting that does not exist yet

lesson.x: A defensible artifact contains the schema, the prompts, the graph structure, the failure log with named errors and fixes, and the commands to reproduce it. A screenshot of a pretty graph contains none of that.
Week 10 gate: is your project better evidence than any credential? If yes, it is done. If it is only prettier, it is a tutorial.

instructions: Two items on what counts as evidence, one on the Week 4 gate.
Partial credit with cancellation on the multi-select: select only what a reviewer could verify.
Read every option as if you were the reviewer deciding whether to trust the person.

exercises.prompt: Which of these make a project count as evidence of real understanding?
options: A failure log naming each error, the fix, and whether the fix held.
The actual extraction schema and resolve prompt, in the repo.
Commands that reproduce the pipeline from a clean checkout.
A screenshot of the finished graph.
A certificate from an online course.
notes: The log is the artifact that distinguishes a builder from someone who ran a tutorial.
Prompts and schema are the design. A reviewer can critique a design.
Reproducibility is the difference between a claim and a result.
A picture shows the output, not the judgment, and it is the one thing that cannot be wrong in a screenshot.
A credential shows attendance. The vault is explicit that the portfolio outperforms it.
exercises.why: Three verifiable artifacts, two signals that prove nothing. What a reviewer needs is the ability to check your work and to see that you can find your own errors.

exercises.prompt: The Week 4 gate asks you to show one extraction error and one resolve error. Why both?
options: Because extraction errors are easy to find and resolve errors are where the real failures hide, so only the second proves you tested the hard stage.
Because they are the same class of error.
Because two examples of each are the requirement.
Because resolve only fails when extract fails.
exercises.why: Anyone can catch a wrong label. The resolve stage is where false and missed merges silently corrupt the graph, so showing you found one there proves you actually inspected the hard part.
wrong: Different stages, different failure classes, different fixes.
The gate asks for one of each caught and fixed, not a quota.
They are independent. A perfect extract still merges two people who share a name.

exercises.prompt: Which of the five stall patterns does a beautiful demo with no failure log represent?
options: Optimising visual polish over honest failure documentation.
Skipping the manual extraction phase.
Building only one half.
Waiting for the job title.
exercises.why: It is the polish trap. The demo is the part that photographs well, so it gets finished first, and the log that would prove understanding never gets written.
wrong: That stall shows up as an extractor you cannot evaluate, not as a polished surface.
One half means no agent layer or no graph, which a demo can still hide.
The job-title stall is about where you apply, not what you built.

modules.title: Measure it honestly
modules.kicker: Precision is cheap, recall is the job
modules.goal: Score an extraction pass so the number cannot be gamed.

lesson.x: Two numbers, opposite directions. Precision: of the triples I emitted, how many are right. Recall: of the triples that exist in the source, how many did I find. Report both, with the gold set size, or you are reporting decoration.
A small worked case

gold set: 50 triples
extractor emitted 40, of which 32 are correct

precision = 32 / 40 = 0.80
recall    = 32 / 50 = 0.64

Eight wrong emissions and eighteen missed facts. The missed facts are invisible in the output: nothing tells you what you failed to extract. That asymmetry is why a team that only reads its own output believes it is at 0.95 when it is at 0.64.
Build the gold set by hand on 30 documents before tuning anything. Without it every prompt change is a vibe check and every quality claim is unfalsifiable.

instructions: One numeric item and two judgement items.
For recall, write a decimal (0.64) or a percentage (64%). Either is accepted, within 0.01.
Wrong answers here are usually arithmetic from the wrong denominator. Read which set is the denominator before you type.

exercises.prompt: Gold set has 50 triples. The extractor emitted 40 triples, 32 of them correct. What is the recall?
exercises.why: Recall is what you found out of what exists: 32 of 50 is 0.64. Precision is 32 of 40, or 0.80. Two thirds of the source's facts never reach the graph, and nothing in the output tells you that.
exercises.hint: Correctly found divided by everything in the gold set.

exercises.prompt: Precision 0.80, recall 0.64. Where is the loss?
options: Coverage: 18 gold triples were never extracted, against 8 emitted triples that were wrong.
The extractor over-emits, so tighten the schema and drop predicates.
The gold set must be wrong, since precision is high.
Precision and recall are the same measure at different thresholds.
exercises.why: Eight bad emissions and eighteen missed facts. The dominant loss is coverage. Tightening the schema would raise precision and cut recall further, making the real gap worse.
wrong: This treats 8 wrong emissions as the problem while 18 missing facts sit unexamined.
High precision says nothing about the gold set, and definitely does not explain 18 missing facts.
They measure opposite error directions: what you emitted against what you found.

exercises.prompt: An extractor reports precision 0.99 by emitting about three triples per document. Is it good?
options: No. Precision is trivially gamed by emitting less, so the claim means nothing without recall and the gold set size.
Yes. 0.99 precision is production quality.
Yes, if those three triples are the important ones.
It depends on the model size.
exercises.why: Emit one triple you are certain of and precision approaches 1.0. The number is uninterpretable alone, which is why the honest report is precision, recall and gold set size together.
wrong: Precision without recall is the cheap half of a scoreboard.
Then show those three cover most of the gold set. Without that, the claim cannot be checked.
Model size does not fix a metric that a narrower output games.
